name: button-design
title: Designing buttons and interactive controls
description: Use when designing, building, restyling, or reviewing any button, CTA, pill, toggle, or tappable control in a mobile or web UI. Applies whenever someone says they are working on a button, adding a new action to a screen, changing what a button says or how it looks, or deciding between primary, secondary, and destructive actions. Covers sizing, labels, states, contrast, and motion for Northwind's payments surfaces where a mis-tapped button moves real money.
body:
- Minimum tap target 44x44pt (iOS) / 48x48dp (Android), even if the visual pill is smaller — pad, don't grow the fill.
- One primary button per screen. Everything else is secondary, tertiary, or a plain text link. If you need two primaries, the screen is doing two jobs.
- Labels are sentence case, verb-first, and name the outcome: "Send $40.00", not "Submit" or "OK". Never end in an ellipsis unless a second confirmation step follows.
- Define all five states before you ship: default, pressed, disabled, loading, and error/retry. Loading replaces the label with a spinner and keeps the button's width fixed so the layout never jumps.
- Money-moving buttons are never disabled silently — if the action can't proceed, keep the button enabled and show the reason on tap. A dead grey button with no explanation is a support ticket.
- Contrast: label vs. fill at 4.5:1 minimum; don't rely on color alone to distinguish destructive actions — pair red with an explicit word like "Cancel payment".
- Press feedback within 100ms. Scale to 0.97 with a 120ms ease-out, or a fill darken of ~8%. No bounce, no spring overshoot on financial actions.
- Destructive and irreversible actions (refund, close account, cancel transfer) require a confirmation sheet, not just a red button.
- Corner radius, height, and horizontal padding come from the design tokens — never hardcode. Height tokens: 52pt full-width, 44pt inline, 32pt compact.
- Full-width buttons sit above the safe area with 16pt side margins and stay pinned, not scrolled away, on any screen where the button is the point of the screen.

name: writing-updates-to-leadership
title: Writing status updates for leadership
description: Use when writing a status update, weekly snippet, exec summary, or any written report going up the chain to a manager, director, or VP. Applies when someone asks to summarize what the team shipped, draft a progress note, prepare for a review, or tell leadership where a project stands. The goal is a short, factual update that lets a busy reader decide something without a follow-up meeting.
body:
- Three headings, always, in this order: Shipped / In flight / Risks. Nothing else.
- Shipped = in production and measurable. If it merged but isn't behind a live flag for real users, it is In flight.
- No adjectives about our own work. Delete "great", "solid", "huge", "significant", "successfully". State the thing and the number.
- Every line carries a number or a date: "Apple Pay checkout live for 100% of US users since Aug 8; auth rate 94.1% (was 91.6%)".
- In flight lines end with a committed date and an owner name. "Soon" and "early next month" are not dates.
- Risks are stated as: the risk, the impact if it lands, and what you need from the reader. If you need nothing, say "no ask".
- Bad news goes first inside Risks and is stated plainly in the first clause. Never bury a slip in a subordinate clause.
- Max 200 words. If it doesn't fit, the update is a doc and the update links to it.
- Never explain how hard something was. Effort is not an outcome.
- Do not editorialize about other teams; describe the dependency and its status only.

name: delegating-work
title: Handing work to a teammate
description: Use when handing a task, project, or investigation to another person — assigning a ticket, writing a handoff note, onboarding someone onto an area, or asking a teammate to take something over. Applies whenever the phrasing is about giving work away, splitting up a project, or getting someone else to own a piece. Focuses on transferring enough context that the person can make decisions without coming back to you.
body:
- Write the handoff as: outcome, why now, constraints, definition of done, deadline, and who decides. Six lines, in that order.
- Delegate the outcome, not the steps. If you specify the steps, you own the result and you have not actually delegated.
- Name one owner. Two owners is zero owners.
- Always give the deadline as a date and say what it's driven by ("Aug 27, before the interchange rate change goes live"). A deadline without a reason gets renegotiated.
- Include the context they can't get from the ticket: the failed prior attempt, the person who cares, the political constraint, the file where the tricky part lives.
- State explicitly what they can decide alone vs. what they must check with you. Default should be "decide alone".
- Give them the escalation path: who to ask when blocked, and how long to be stuck before asking ("more than half a day, ping me").
- Set one checkpoint before the deadline, not a stream of check-ins. Put it on the calendar at handoff time.
- Hand over access at the same moment as the work — repo, dashboard, on-call rotation, vendor console. Missing access is the number one silent stall.
- After handoff, route questions about the work to them in public, not through you. Re-answering makes you the owner again.

name: incident-response
title: Running a production incident
description: Use when production is broken or degrading — an outage, a paging alert, a spike in failed payments, elevated error rates, a bad deploy, or anything someone calls a sev. Applies when the request is about responding to a live problem, coordinating a fire, deciding whether to roll back, or writing the postmortem afterward. Prioritizes stopping customer impact over understanding root cause.
body:
- First responder is Incident Commander until they explicitly hand it off by name in the channel. The IC coordinates and does not debug.
- Open the incident channel and declare severity in the first two minutes. Sev1 = money is not moving or is moving wrongly. Sev2 = degraded but transacting. When unsure, call the higher one; downgrading is cheap.
- Order of operations, strictly: stop the bleeding, then confirm it stopped, then diagnose. Never invert this to satisfy curiosity.
- Stop-the-bleeding menu in preference order: flip the feature flag, roll back the deploy, fail over the region, rate-limit the caller, disable the endpoint. Roll back before you understand why — the revert is not the investigation.
- Assign three named roles out loud: IC, comms, and one hands-on-keyboard operator. Everyone else observes and does not type in prod.
- Post a timestamped update every 20 minutes even when nothing has changed. "No change, still investigating, next update 14:20" is a valid update.
- Log every action taken in the channel as you take it, with timestamps. That log is the postmortem timeline.
- One person touches prod at a time and announces each command before running it. Concurrent mitigations create the second incident.
- For payments specifically: quantify stuck/duplicated/failed transactions before declaring all-clear, and open the reconciliation task in the same breath as resolving.
- Postmortem within three business days, blameless, with action items that have owners and dates. "Be more careful" is not an action item.

name: code-review-tone
title: Reviewing a teammate's code
description: Use when reviewing a pull request, leaving comments on someone else's code, or deciding whether to approve, block, or nit. Applies when the request is about giving feedback on a diff, being a reviewer, or figuring out how blunt to be in a comment. Also applies when responding to review feedback received on your own change.
body:
- Block only on: correctness, security, data/money loss, a public API you can't change later, and missing tests for new branching logic. Everything else is non-blocking.
- Prefix every non-blocking comment with "nit:" or "optional:" and mean it — never re-raise a nit after approval.
- Style is the formatter's job. If you're commenting on spacing, quotes, or import order, fix the linter instead.
- Comment on the code, never the author. "This retries non-idempotent charges" not "you forgot idempotency".
- Ask a real question when you don't understand; assert only when you're sure. "What happens if the webhook arrives twice here?" beats a confident wrong claim.
- Give one concrete alternative with any objection. A rejection without a suggested path is a stall.
- Praise exactly what's worth copying, specifically and rarely. Blanket "LGTM nice work" carries no information.
- Approve with comments when the remaining items are nits — don't hold a PR hostage to your preferences.
- Cap the review at what fits in one sitting; if the diff is over ~400 lines, ask for it to be split rather than skimming and approving.
- Architecture disagreements move to a call or a doc after two round-trips in the thread. Long comment wars are a smell, not diligence.

name: swiftui-component-conventions
title: Building SwiftUI components the Northwind way
description: Use when writing, refactoring, or reviewing SwiftUI views and reusable components for the Northwind iOS app — adding a new screen, extracting a component, styling a control, or wiring state into a view. Applies to questions about view composition, styles vs. modifiers, previews, spacing values, and how components should be shared across features.
body:
- Style controls with a `ButtonStyle` / `LabelStyle` / `ToggleStyle` conformance, never a stack of ad-hoc modifiers at the call site. Call sites should read `Button("Send") { }.buttonStyle(.northwindPrimary)`.
- No magic numbers. Every spacing, radius, duration, and color comes from `Theme.spacing.*`, `Theme.radius.*`, `Theme.motion.*`, `Theme.color.*`. A raw `16` in a view is a review comment.
- Every shared component ships with at least three `#Preview` blocks: default, dark mode, and the worst-case content (longest string, largest Dynamic Type, loading state).
- Views take data, not view models, wherever possible. A component that can be previewed with a struct literal is a component that can be tested.
- Keep `body` under ~50 lines. Extract to private computed properties or child views, and pass explicit parameters rather than reaching into the environment from deep leaves.
- `@State` is private and value-typed; shared mutable state uses `@Observable` models injected once at the feature root. No singletons reached from inside a view.
- Components never format money themselves — use `CurrencyFormatter` so locale, sign, and rounding stay consistent everywhere.
- Feature-local views live beside the feature; a view only moves into `DesignSystem/` when a second feature actually needs it. Premature promotion creates parameters nobody uses.
- Accessibility is part of done: label, trait, and a combined element for composite rows. Test one screen per PR at the largest Dynamic Type size.
- Animate explicit values with `withAnimation` on state changes, not `.animation()` on the whole view tree; durations come from motion tokens (fast 120ms, base 200ms, slow 320ms).

name: api-error-handling
title: Handling API failures, retries, and idempotency
description: Use when writing or reviewing code that calls a network API or handles its failures — retries, timeouts, backoff, idempotency keys, webhook processing, error mapping, or what to show the user when a request fails. Especially applies to payment, charge, refund, and transfer calls where a retry can move money twice. Also applies when deciding the wording of a user-facing error.
body:
- Every mutating request carries a client-generated idempotency key (UUIDv4) that is stable across retries of the same user intent and regenerated only on a new intent. Persist the key with the pending record before sending.
- Retry only idempotent or idempotency-keyed calls. Never blind-retry a POST that lacks a key — treat it as unknown-outcome and reconcile instead.
- Retry policy: max 3 attempts, exponential backoff starting at 250ms with full jitter, hard cap at ~8s total. Retry on 408/429/5xx and transport errors only. Never retry 4xx other than 408/429.
- Honor `Retry-After` when present; it outranks your backoff math.
- Timeouts are explicit per call: 10s connect+read for interactive requests, 30s for background reconciliation. There is no such thing as a default timeout you didn't choose.
- Unknown outcome (timeout, connection reset after send) is its own state — not success, not failure. Mark the record `pending_unknown`, then resolve by GET on the idempotency key or by webhook. Never guess.
- Map upstream errors to a small internal enum (`declined`, `insufficient_funds`, `expired_card`, `network`, `rate_limited`, `internal`) at the boundary. Feature code never branches on raw provider strings or HTTP codes.
- User-facing messages say what happened, whether money moved, and the one next action: "We couldn't reach your bank. No money left your account. Try again in a minute." Never surface a status code, stack trace, or provider error name.
- Log the request id, idempotency key, attempt number, and latency on every attempt; never log the PAN, CVV, or full auth token.
- Webhooks are at-least-once: verify the signature, dedupe on event id, and make handlers idempotent. Handlers ack fast and do the work asynchronously.

name: naming-things
title: Naming files, functions, and feature flags
description: Use when choosing or changing a name — a file, module, function, variable, database field, endpoint, branch, or feature flag. Applies when someone asks what to call something, wants a rename suggestion, is setting up a new flag or experiment, or is bikeshedding a term with a teammate. Aims for names that are searchable, predictable, and safe to delete later.
body:
- Name for what the thing is to its caller, not how it works inside. `refundPayment` not `postReversalToLedger`.
- Functions are verb phrases; booleans read as assertions (`isSettled`, `hasPendingRefund`); collections are plural. Avoid `data`, `info`, `manager`, `helper`, `utils` — they mean nothing and become junk drawers.
- Spell it out. `transactionCount` not `txnCnt`. The only allowed abbreviations are the ones in the glossary: `id`, `url`, `api`, `pan`, `kyc`.
- Feature flags: `<team>_<feature>_<verb>`, lowercase snake, e.g. `payments_applepay_enabled`. Every flag has an owner and a removal date recorded at creation.
- Flags describe the new behavior in the affirmative and default to off. Never a double negative (`disable_no_legacy_flow` is banned).
- Kill-switches are named `*_killswitch`, default on, and are exempt from the removal date — but they must be documented in the runbook.
- Files match the primary type they export; one public type per file. Swift files use `UpperCamelCase.swift`, scripts and configs use `kebab-case`.
- Branches: `<user>/<area>-<short-desc>`, e.g. `sam/checkout-retry-backoff`. Never `fix`, `wip`, or a bare ticket number.
- Money fields carry their unit and currency handling in the name: `amountMinorUnits`, `feeMinorUnits`. A field named `amount` will eventually be off by 100.
- If a name needs a comment to explain it, rename it instead. Renaming is cheap before merge and expensive after — argue about it in the PR, not in six months.
